Latin. The language of ancient Rome and the Roman Empire, which evolved from a regional Italic dialect into the administrative, literary, and ceremonial tongue of one of history's greatest civilizations. Spoken by ordinary Romans and refined by educated elites into Classical Latin, it became the vehicle for Roman law, philosophy, rhetoric, and poetry that shaped Western intellectual tradition.

As Roman power expanded, Latin replaced local languages across conquered territories, becoming the lingua franca of the empire. Classical Latin, the refined literary form perfected by authors like Virgil, Cicero, and Livy, differs markedly from Vulgar Latin, the spoken dialect of common Romans, from which the Romance languages ultimately descended.

After Rome's fall, Latin persisted as the language of the medieval Church. The Vulgate, St. Jerome's late-fourth-century translation of the Bible into Latin, preserved and sanctified the language as the language of Christian theology and made it the official liturgical language of the Roman Catholic Church for over fifteen hundred years.

Latin employed a complex system of cases, declensions, and conjugations to encode grammatical relationships. As the Roman Empire fell, spoken Latin evolved into regional variants influenced by local languages. By the eighth century, these had developed into distinct Romance languages, a transition that took centuries. Medieval and Renaissance scholars maintained Latin as the international language of learning, theology, medicine, and law, making it the backbone of European intellectual continuity.

Modern scientific nomenclature, biological taxonomy, anatomical terms, and chemical compounds all employ Latin-based terminology, preserving its role as a precision language for technical and scholarly discourse. Latin shares ancestry with ancient Rome, the civilization whose language it was, and connects to the Romance languages that descended from it, the Vulgate Bible that preserved it, and the broader linguistic development of Europe.
